guideTitle: 6 Best Fruit Pickers for Mangoes in 2026
metaTitle: Best Fruit Pickers for Mangoes in 2026
metaDescription: Six mango pickers compared, from a blade-and-net harvesting head to long steel and aluminum poles, so you can collect heavy fruit from the ground.
introParagraphs: Mangoes are a different problem from apples. The fruit is heavier, the trees are far taller, and the stem leaks a sticky sap when it is torn rather than cut. A tool that works well for a pear can leave you wrestling a loaded basket at the end of a long pole, or rubbing sap off your forearms. The right picker for a mango tree has real reach, a basket that holds weight without folding, and a method that treats the stem gently.

The six picks here cover two different approaches. The PEAKHILL harvester is a blade-and-net head with four replaceable stainless steel blades and a 10 inch nylon collection basket, sold without a pole. The DonSail 35 to 120 inch, Walensee 13FT and BlumeTrec 13.5FT are stainless steel pole-and-basket kits. The SKGPOLE and TONYINGO 30FT are aluminum telescoping poles that run past 20 feet, which is where many mango trees actually need you to reach.

We evaluated each pick from its listing specs and typical buyer feedback, so lengths and materials are as the makers describe them. Every long pole here is metal and conducts electricity, so check for overhead wires before you extend anything. A mango tree near a service line is a job for a professional, not for a longer pole.

products.name: Walensee 13FT Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The Walensee 13FT is named a mango picker in its own title, and its specs back that up. The pole extends from 35 to 158 inches, which is nearly 13 and a half feet of shaft, and the basket carries a cushioned foam pad that absorbs the impact when a heavy fruit drops in. The shaft is described as reinforced stainless steel, a sensible choice when a mango can weigh far more than an apple.

The cushioned basket matters more for mangoes than for lighter fruit. A ripe mango has soft flesh just under the skin, and a hard landing at the bottom of an unpadded steel basket leaves a dark bruise that spreads fast. The foam pad also reduces the clatter when fruit lands, which helps if you are working beneath a tree that other fruit is still hanging from. The steel shaft feels stiff, so the basket stays where you aim it.

The limitation is the usual one for long steel: handling at full extension. Compared with the TONYINGO 30FT, the Walensee reaches about half as far but weighs less than a comparable steel pole would at the same length, and it is easier to steer. Compared with the BlumeTrec 13.5FT, it gives up about 3 inches of height. Keep it dry between uses, and keep every inch of it away from overhead lines.
products.bestFor: Backyard mango trees up to roughly 16 feet where fruit needs a cushioned landing.
pros: Cushioned foam pad protects soft mango flesh
Reaches 158 inches from the ground
Reinforced stainless steel feels stiff
Named for mangoes in the listing
cons: Heavy at the tip with several mangoes

products.name: TONYINGO 30FT Reach Fruit Picker with Basket
products.description:
Mature mango trees are often tall enough that a 13 foot pole simply will not reach the crown. The TONYINGO 30FT is the longest pole in this guide: a 5 to 24 foot aluminum alloy telescoping shaft with a maker-stated reach of 30 feet once your height is added. It locks at six adjustable heights, which gives you stops along the way rather than a single extend-or-collapse choice.

Its locking system is the other reason it stands out. The listing describes a dual flip-lock and screw fixing design, so each section is clamped and then screwed in place, a belt-and-braces approach for a pole that is carrying a heavy fruit at height. The metal basket has a bowl-shaped sponge pad at the bottom that cushions the landing, and the aluminum alloy comes with a corrosion-resistant coating, which is useful if the pole is kept in a humid garage.

The tradeoff is leverage. A 24 foot pole with a full mango at the end is hard to control, and you need to keep both hands firmly on the shaft. It is also the one most dangerous near power lines, because aluminum conducts electricity extremely well. Compared with the SKGPOLE, which is also aluminum but tops out at 20 feet, the TONYINGO adds 4 more feet of range. Extend only what you need, and lower the pole before emptying the basket.
products.bestFor: Tall mature mango trees where fruit hangs 20 feet or more above the ground.
pros: Reaches up to 24 feet of pole length
Six locking heights give fine control
Dual flip-lock and screw fixing holds firm
Sponge pad cushions heavy fruit
cons: Very long pole is tiring to hold steady
Aluminum is a serious conductor near wires

products.name: PEAKHILL Mango Fruit Picker Harvester Head
products.description:
The PEAKHILL is a different tool from the other five. Rather than a wire-and-foam basket that twists the stem off, it is a harvester head with four replaceable stainless steel blades, each about 4 inches long, and a soft nylon collection basket of 10 inches. It is sold without a pole, so it suits someone who already owns a long extension pole and wants a cutting head rather than a twisting one.

Cutting has a real advantage with mangoes. Pulling or twisting a mango can tear the stem and release sap, whereas a clean cut leaves a short stem on the fruit. The listing says the blades give clean cuts that protect the tree's health, and the nylon basket catches the mango in mid-air to reduce drops. A soft net is also gentler than a rigid metal basket on ripe fruit.

The two cautions are the missing pole and the sharp blades. You must supply a compatible pole, so check the fit before buying, and you must handle the head with care when it is not attached. Compared with the Walensee, which gives you both pole and basket, the PEAKHILL is a cheaper add-on if you have the shaft already. Replace the blades when they dull, and store the head with a cover on the cutting edges.
products.bestFor: Owners who already have an extension pole and want a stem-cutting head for mangoes.
pros: Four replaceable blades make clean cuts
Soft nylon basket catches fruit mid-air
10 inch basket holds a large mango
No pole cost if you own one
cons: Pole is not included in the listing

products.name: BlumeTrec 13.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
products.description:
The BlumeTrec 13.5FT extends from 35 to 161 inches in sections of 16 inches each, and the maker markets it as a long-handle mango grabber. The sectional build means no sliding lock to fail under the weight of a mango, and you can add or remove pieces to suit the branch. A thick foam pad lines the bottom of the basket to soften the landing.

For mango picking, the fixed sections give you a secure feel. A large mango can weigh as much as a small bag of flour, and a telescoping lock that creeps under that load is more than an annoyance. With a sectional steel shaft you set the length once and know it will not move. The pole is stainless steel, so it resists rust better than a plain steel shaft, though you should still wipe off the sticky sap before storage.

It costs you in weight at full height. A 161 inch steel pole is heavier than the Walensee at 158 inches by only a small margin, but the TONYINGO and SKGPOLE are lighter at similar lengths. If you can reach your fruit with 13 feet of pole, the BlumeTrec is a solid, secure choice. If you need to go higher, choose an aluminum telescoping model instead. Keep it away from wires, and clean mango sap from each section before it dries.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who want a locked-in, non-sliding pole for heavy mangoes up to about 16 feet.
pros: Sectional build has no sliding lock
Reach to 161 inches
Foam pad softens the landing
Stainless steel resists rust
cons: Heavier than aluminum at the same reach

products.name: DonSail Fruit Picker Pole, 35 to 120 Inch
products.description:
The DonSail 35 to 120 inch model sits between the short and long ends of this lineup. At 120 inches it is exactly 10 feet of pole, which is enough for a medium mango tree or the lower half of a large one. The shaft is a thick 1 inch stainless steel tube, and the twist-on metal basket measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches. The maker calls it a mango picker in the title.

The basket is roomy enough for a standard mango, and the thick shaft gives you a stable feel when you tilt the head against a branch. The sectional design is easier to control than a telescoping pole at a similar length, since it does not flex at the joints. Compared with the Walensee at 158 inches, the DonSail stops about 4 feet lower, but it is noticeably easier to carry and aim.

The downside is the lack of cushioning detail. The listing describes a metal basket without mentioning foam padding, so the fall into the basket is harder, and a ripe mango can bruise. If bruising worries you, lay a clean cloth in the basket, or choose the Walensee or BlumeTrec instead. Wipe the sap from the shaft after each session and keep the wire dry to prevent rust.
products.bestFor: Medium mango trees or the lower branches of tall ones, reached from a stable stance.
pros: 120 inches is enough for many backyard trees
Thick 1 inch steel shaft is stable
Big basket fits a standard mango
Sectional pieces have no sliding locks
cons: Cannot reach the crown of a tall tree

products.name: SKGPOLE 26FT Reach Fruit Picker
products.description:
The SKGPOLE is the lighter alternative to a steel pole when the mango tree is tall. It is a telescoping aluminum pole running 5 to 20 feet, with a maker-claimed reach of 26 feet, a metal twist-on basket of 5.5 inches in diameter, and an ultra thick foam pad. The thread is a 3/4 inch American standard, so you can fit another head later, including a cutting head like the PEAKHILL if the thread matches.

A lightweight aluminum shaft changes how a long session feels. Where a steel pole tires your shoulders at 12 feet, aluminum stays comfortable well beyond that. The foam pad is a thick one, which is welcome for soft fruit. The smaller basket is a plus and a minus: it keeps the tip lighter, but it holds only one or two mangoes before you must lower it.

Compared with the TONYINGO, the SKGPOLE reaches 4 feet less but has a clearer listing about thread compatibility and padding. Compared with the Walensee, it reaches much higher at similar handling effort, but it flexes more at full extension. Check the locks before you lift, treat the aluminum as a conductor near power lines, and wipe sap from the sections to keep them sliding smoothly.
products.bestFor: Tall mango trees where lighter weight and a standard thread for swapping heads both matter.
pros: Reaches 20 feet of pole length
Aluminum is lighter than steel
Thick foam pad cushions fruit
Standard thread supports swapping heads
cons: Small basket holds only a mango or two

buyingCriteria.explanation: Unpruned mango trees can grow far taller than most home fruit trees, so reach is the first filter. A pole of 10 feet, such as the DonSail at 120 inches, suits a pruned or medium tree. The Walensee at 158 inches and BlumeTrec at 161 inches suit trees up to about 16 feet. Beyond that, only the SKGPOLE at up to 20 feet and the TONYINGO at up to 24 feet of pole offer the length. Subtract about 6 feet for your own standing reach, and buy a pole one section longer than the math suggests.

A mango is heavy compared with an apple or an orange, and the weight sits at the far end of the pole, where it creates the most leverage. A steel sectional pole, like the BlumeTrec, holds firm under that load. A telescoping aluminum pole, like the TONYINGO, is lighter overall but flexes when a full mango is added. Always lower the pole before removing fruit, and never swing a loaded basket sideways.

Mango stems release a milky sap that can irritate skin and stain the fruit if the stem is torn. Cutting the stem cleanly, as the PEAKHILL blades do, is gentler than twisting it off in a wire basket. If you use a twist-style basket, leave a short stem on the mango and let the sap drain stem-down on a rack. Wear gloves and long sleeves when you work beneath the tree.

Mango flesh is soft just under the skin, and impact bruising turns it brown within a day. The Walensee, BlumeTrec 13.5FT, TONYINGO and SKGPOLE all list foam or sponge padding in the basket, and the PEAKHILL uses a soft nylon net. The DonSail 120 inch pole lists a metal basket without padding, so add a soft liner if you buy it. Padding is a better investment than a few extra inches of reach.

The TONYINGO uses a dual flip-lock and screw fixing at six heights, which is the most secure locking system in this lineup. The SKGPOLE uses a telescoping lock, and the steel sectional poles avoid sliding joints altogether. A mango and basket together can weigh several pounds, so test every lock with a firm downward tug before you lift. Never use a pole whose lock slips even a little.

All the long poles in this guide are metal, and mango trees are often grown near houses and service lines. Look up before every session, keep the pole at least three metres, or about ten feet, from any wire, and never use it in damp weather near one. A 24 foot aluminum pole can reach a wire far more easily than you expect. If your tree touches a wire, call the utility.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach for large trees
howWeEvaluated.description: Mango trees need more reach than most fruit trees, so we compared maximum pole length. The TONYINGO leads at up to 24 feet of pole, followed by the SKGPOLE at 20 feet, the BlumeTrec at 161 inches, the Walensee at 158 inches and the DonSail at 120 inches. The PEAKHILL has no pole, so it was judged on its head design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fruit cushioning
howWeEvaluated.description: Soft ripe mangoes bruise easily, so we looked at basket padding. The Walensee, BlumeTrec, SKGPOLE and TONYINGO list foam or sponge pads, and the PEAKHILL uses a nylon net. The DonSail was marked down because its listing mentions a metal basket with no padding.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and leverage
howWeEvaluated.description: A heavy fruit at the end of a long pole creates strain, so we compared steel sectional poles with aluminum telescoping poles. The aluminum SKGPOLE and TONYINGO score best for weight at length, while the steel DonSail, BlumeTrec and Walensee score best for stiffness.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lock and joint design
howWeEvaluated.description: We read how each pole holds its length. The TONYINGO's dual flip-lock and screw design and the sectional steel poles earned top marks for security, while simple telescoping locks need more frequent checks with a heavy load.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stem and sap handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Because mango sap is a real nuisance, we looked at how each tool detaches the fruit. The PEAKHILL cuts the stem with four replaceable blades, while the pole-and-basket kits twist the stem free. The cutting approach is cleaner, but the twist approach is simpler and includes the pole.

howToChoose.intro: Measure the height of the highest fruit you want, subtract about 6 feet for your own reach, and choose a pole at least that long.

howToChoose.intro: Two different mechanisms detach a mango from its branch, and each has a clear user.

cards.label: Cutting head
cards.text: A blade head cuts the stem cleanly, and the net catches the fruit as it falls. The PEAKHILL is the only cutting tool here, with four replaceable stainless blades of about 4 inches. It leaves a short stem on the mango and avoids tearing. The downside is that you need a compatible pole and must respect the blades.

cards.label: Twisting basket
cards.text: A wire or metal basket lifts and twists the stem free. The Walensee, BlumeTrec, DonSail, SKGPOLE and TONYINGO all work this way. It is simpler, includes the pole and works on many fruits, but a hard twist can tear the stem. Choose the PEAKHILL if you want clean cuts, and one of the pole-and-basket kits if you want an all-in-one tool.

howToChoose.note: A taller pole is only worth it if you can hold it steadily. If in doubt, prune the tree to a height your pole can reach.

faq.q: How do I pick mangoes without getting sap on my skin?
faq.a: Wear long sleeves and gloves, and pick so the sap drains away from you. Leave a short stem on each mango and place it stem-down on a rack or a sheet of cardboard for a few hours. A cutting head such as the PEAKHILL makes a clean cut that reduces tearing. Wash any sap off your skin promptly, because it can cause irritation in some people.

faq.q: Which mango picker has the longest reach?
faq.a: The TONYINGO 30FT has the longest pole at 5 to 24 feet, with a maker-stated total reach of 30 feet. The SKGPOLE follows at 5 to 20 feet. The BlumeTrec at 161 inches and the Walensee at 158 inches reach about 13 feet of pole. Longer is not always better, because a long pole with a heavy mango is tiring to control.

faq.q: Is steel or aluminum better for heavy mangoes?
faq.a: Steel, as on the DonSail, Walensee and BlumeTrec, resists flex and keeps the basket where you aim it. Aluminum, as on the SKGPOLE and TONYINGO, is lighter and wins when the pole is very long. For trees under 14 feet, steel is usually the more comfortable option. For tall trees, aluminum is the only realistic way to hold the pole up for more than a few minutes.

faq.q: Can a fruit picker handle large mangoes?
faq.a: Most baskets suit standard-size mangoes. The DonSail basket is about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches and the PEAKHILL net is 10 inches, both fine for an ordinary fruit. Very large varieties may need two hands and a slower approach, so lift gently and lower the pole between fruits. A small basket like the SKGPOLE at 5.5 inches suits one fruit at a time.

faq.q: Is it safe to use these poles near power lines?
faq.a: No. Steel and aluminum both conduct electricity, and long poles can reach a wire much more easily than you expect. Keep at least three metres, about ten feet, away from any overhead line, and stay out of wet conditions. If your mango tree grows near a wire, call the utility or a professional tree service, and do not try to move branches yourself.

faq.q: How do I care for the pole after picking mangoes?
faq.a: Rinse or wipe off any sap while it is still wet, because dried mango sap makes telescoping joints stick. Let the pole dry completely before storage, and hang it or lay it flat. Check the basket wire for rust and the foam for wear each season. Replace the PEAKHILL blades when they stop cutting cleanly.

faq.q: Should I pick mangoes ripe or slightly early?
faq.a: Many growers pick mangoes when they are mature but still firm and let them ripen indoors, because fully ripe fruit bruises on a hard landing. A mango that has a full shoulder and a slight color change at the stem end is usually ready. Let them sit at room temperature for a few days, and move them to the fridge once they give slightly to pressure.
